description: A fast 2D and 3D game engine — TypeScript SDK, C++/WebAssembly core, visual editor. Ship one project to web, desktop, WeChat MiniGames, playable ads, and native Android / iOS.

latest_release.name: v0.116.0
latest_release.body:
### Added

- **A stop clip can land where the character stops.** An animator state gains `distanceParameter`: a float saying how far the character has left to go, and the state is played by it, standing each frame at the point of its clip with that much root travel left, so however hard the character brakes its feet come to rest where it does. Under `distanceFloor` world units it plays on by time, and it never runs more than `distanceMaxPace` times its own pace in a frame. For such clips a model's import settings gain Root Motion, From the Skeleton, Its Own Pace, which takes the top joint's course key by key instead of at a steady rate, so a clip that brakes keeps its braking in the root track. The animator's details now show every setting a state and a constraint take, the stride and orientation warps' `ease` among them.
- **An animator transition can blend by inertia instead of crossfading.** A transition's `blend`, or a controller's `transitionBlend` for every transition that does not say, takes `inertialize`: the state entered plays at once, and each joint's offset from where the last frame left it is carried down to nothing over the transition's duration along a curve that starts with the speed the joint had and arrives with none. The character is never in two motions at once, so a foot does not skim the ground between two gaits' footfalls. It applies to the base layer. On the character it was made for, starting to walk slid a planted foot 3.9 units against 17.8 crossfaded. A stride warp also no longer lets a stride back out to the clip's on the last frame a character moves before it stops.
- **Luban builds a client and a server from the same tables.** The project's Luban settings take a list of outputs: each names a target of `luban.conf` (`client`, `server`, …) and the folders its code and data are written to, so a game whose server reads tables the client never ships gets both from one run. Settings → Configuration tables shows them as a table with a row per output. Luban runs once per output and writes nothing until every one has worked; a project written with one target, code folder and data folder reads as that one output.
- **WeChat and Douyin mini-games can run 3D physics with Jolt or PhysX.** Exports package the project's selected 3D solver and add Box2D when the game also uses 2D physics. With engine subpackaging enabled, each optional engine binary downloads on first use and stays outside the main-package budget. The exporter names the matching build command for a missing or Web-only solver. A targeted build restores missing files and syncs its selected runtime to the editor.
- **A character going a different way from the one it faces runs with its legs that way.** An animator's constraints gain Legs follow movement (`orientation-warp`): the animator measures the angle between the way the character goes over the ground and the way its motion travels, and the constraint turns the hips by it (within `maxAngle`, 90 degrees by default) and the listed spine joints back by as much, so the chest keeps facing where the character faces. It matters when facing and movement part: a body that turns slower than the way it goes, strafing, aiming. Measured on a run with a body turning at 60 degrees a second, a planted toe slid 50 units through two turns with it and 69 without.
- **A character can cover ground by its animation's own travel, so its feet do not slide.** Three pieces, each usable alone. A model's import settings gain Root Motion, From the Skeleton: for a rig with no root above the hips, each clip's travel over the ground is taken out of the top joint and stated as a root track at one steady rate, and a clip that ends where it began is left alone. An Animator gains Rig, the entity whose children its clips pose, for a character that carries its model as a child. A Third Person Controller gains Root Motion: the stick then chooses the heading and the speed it asks the animator for, and the gait that answers is what

detail.readme:
# Estella **A 2D and 3D game engine whose editor is an MCP server.**
Your AI agent builds the game with the same 181 tools the editor's own UI uses — then ships it to the web, mini-game platforms, playable ads, desktop and native mobile. [![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/esengine/estella)](https://github.com/esengine/estella/releases) [![MCP](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-181_tools-8A2BE2.svg)](https://estellaengine.com/docs/agents/mcp/) [![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/Platform-Web%20%7C%20Mini--games%20%7C%20Playable%20ads%20%7C%20Desktop%20%7C%20Android%20%7C%20iOS-green.svg)](https://estellaengine.com/docs/publishing/overview/) [![Ask DeepWiki](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ask-DeepWiki-1f6feb.svg)](https://deepwiki.com/esengine/estella) [Website](https://estellaengine.com)  ·  [Agent](#your-agent-drives-the-editor)  ·  [Getting Started](#getting-started)  ·  [Documentation](#documentation)  ·  [QQ群 481923584](https://qm.qq.com/q/BONa5LXQ0U)
Every frame is one MCP tool call into the editor, captured as it happened — no mouse involved.
## Your agent drives the editor The Estella editor speaks the **Model Context Protocol**. Connect Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or any MCP client, and the agent works inside the real editor rather than around it: - **It builds** — creates projects, spawns entities from the editor's own Create catalog, writes component fields, makes prefabs, paints tilemaps, writes and type-checks scripts. - **It looks** — takes screenshots of the viewport and the running game, replays a frame draw by draw, compares the game with reference images, and audits what a scene's look lacks. - **It plays** — enters Play mode, steps time deterministically, sends input and clicks UI by name, runs scripted playtests, then reads the running world back. - **It makes assets** — images, sound effects, music and 3D models, each answered with a picture of what it made. - **It ships** — reads project health, exports the game, and drives a build running on a connected phone. Every call goes through the editor's command surface: each one is **one undo step**, you watch it happen in the window, and you can take the mouse back at any time. The editor starts **read-only**; an agent edits only after you allow it in *Window → Connect AI Tools…*, which also writes the client's MCP config for you. **The tools are not all loaded at once.** A session starts with the everyday ones only, about fifty: read and edit the scene, play and step the game, open and save, screenshots, logs, undo. The rest sit in the groups below, and the agent lists a group when the work calls for it (`enable_tools { groups: ["look"] }`), so a session does not pay thousands of tokens of tool descriptions for tools it never uses. Long tool guides work the same way: a description is the short form, and `tool_guide` reads the rest by topic. How a kind of task is done end to end (2D and 3D gameplay, UI, animation, multiplayer, performance, shipping) is a skill the agent reads with `skill_guide` before it starts. | Group | What the agent gets | |---|---| | core | scene tree, entities, components, play / step / input, screenshots, logs, undo | | `assets` · `prefab` · `authoring` | asset documents and import settings, tilemaps, prefabs and variants, physics bodies, UI events | | `look` · `render` | reference images beside the game, light and field sweeps, frame capture and replay, shadows, LOD, bakes | | `code` · `project` | scripts, symbol search, type-check, project settings, health, export | | `image` · `sound` · `modeling` | draw sprites and textures, compose sound and music, build 3D models from steps | | `terrain` · `tripo` | shape land from steps (ranges, rivers, roads, a coast) and place it in the scene; generate textured 3D models with Tripo AI (your own key and credits) | | `play` · `view` · `device` | gamepads, time scale, scripted playtests, editor view, and a game running on a connected phone | **How undo works.** Tools are sorted by how their effect is taken back, not by what they touch: | A call that… | is taken back by | |---|---| | reads (scene tree, screenshots, logs, stats) | nothing to take back | | plays, steps or sends input to the game | **Stop**: the game runs in its own copy of the world and never touches the scene you edit | | edits the scene or a prefab | **Undo**: the edit goes through the editor's own history, the one Ctrl+Z walks | | writes project files (a script, an asset, an image, a material) | **Undo** as well: the editor keeps each file as it was before the call and puts it back | | leaves the project or runs code nobody can enumerate (a new project, an export, an editor command, code evaluated in the running game) | not undoable, and marked so | One call is one step however much it did: a tool that adds six entities and writes two files is undone by a single Undo, by you with Ctrl+Z or by the agent with its `undo` tool. A save is not a step, so undoing never rolls a saved file back under an unchanged scene. → [Connecting an agent](https://estellaengine.com/docs/agents/mcp/) ## Why Estella, when Unity and Unreal have MCP too? An MCP server can be bolted onto any editor. What an agent can actually get done depends on what sits behind it. - **The protocol is the editor, not a plugin on it.** The 181 tools call the pipelines the editor's own menus, inspector and toolbar run, so an agent's edit is the edit a person would have made, and undoes the same way. Calls are schema-checked and permission-gated by the editor itself. - **The agent can check its own work.** It steps a paused game frame by frame, so "play three seconds, then look" is the same frame every run. It sees the game, not just the log: screenshots, a frame replayed draw call by draw call, the game set beside a reference image, scripted playtests that read the running world back. - **The agent can make what the game needs.** Sprites, textures, sound effects, music and 3D models come from tools inside the editor, so a prototype does not stop at grey boxes while someone opens five other programs. - **Everything is text.** Scenes, prefabs and materials are JSON; gameplay is TypeScript. An agent reads and writes the project directly, and every change is a reviewable diff. - **It ships where heavier engines struggle.** A WebAssembly runtime that loads on a phone browser, seven Chinese mini-game platforms, single-file playable ads for the major ad networks, and native Android / iOS apps — from one project. - **It is open.** The runtime, SDK, pipeline and CLI are Apache-2.0: no royalties, no seats, no runtime fees. The editor is a free download. ## Rendered in real time

One day on the Amazon Lumberyard Bistro, recorded frame by frame from the running game: a sun that follows the clock, weather that turns from clear to mist, rain and snow, baked bounce light, reflections and volumetric haze. Scene © Amazon Lumberyard, CC BY 4.0, modified.

Space Frigate, a game made with Estella and recorded frame by frame as it runs: flying on thrusters, gunnery, and a jump through a gate to another star system. Every model, texture and sound in it is generated from a recipe.

A fight scene an AI agent built in the editor through MCP, recorded frame by frame as it runs. Both characters, their rigs and animations, the columns, the braziers and the floor texture were generated with Tripo AI by the editor's tripo tools.
## What's inside Estella is a C++ engine with a TypeScript SDK. The core runs as WebAssembly on the web and natively on desktop and mobile; game logic is written as ECS systems in TypeScript. **2D** — sprites and sprite animation, tilemaps (with LDtk import), Spine 2.1 – 4.3 and DragonBones, 2D lights and shadows, UI with layout, rich and bitmap text, particles, Box2D physics, native 2D rigs. **3D** — glTF / FBX import, PBR materials, directional / point / spot lights with shadows, sky atmosphere with time of day and weather, baked lightmaps, light and reflection probes, SSR, SSGI, height fog, terrain, water, foliage, skeletal animation with spring bones, navigation, Jolt or PhysX physics, streamed large worlds. **Everywhere** — one renderer for 2D and 3D on WebGL 2 and WebGPU, and one project exports to: | Target | What you get | |---|---| | Web | a static, self-contained build | | Mini-games | WeChat, Douyin, Kuaishou, Bilibili, Alipay, Huawei and quick games | | Playable ads | one inlined `index.html` for Meta, Google, Unity, AppLovin, Mintegral, TikTok / Pangle and MRAID networks | | Desktop | a native app on Windows, macOS and Linux — no Chromium | | Android / iOS | a native arm64 app on Vulkan / Metal — not a WebView | ## Getting Started **Install.** Download the editor for Windows or macOS from [estellaengine.com](https://estellaengine.com/#download) — always the newest release. Every build is also on the [releases page](https://github.com/esengine/estella/releases). **Create a project.** Open the editor, click **New Project**, pick a template. **Write a system.** ```typescript import { defineComponent, defineSystem, addSystem, Query, Mut, Res, Time, LocalTransform } from 'esengine'; const Speed = defineComponent('Speed', { value: 200 }); addSystem(defineSystem( [Res(Time), Query(Mut(LocalTransform), Speed)], (time, query) => { for (const [entity, transform, speed] of query) { transform.position.x += speed.value * time.delta; } } )); ``` Press **F5** to play — or connect your agent and ask it to do all three. ## Documentation Everything lives at [estellaengine.com/docs](https://estellaengine.com/docs). | | Start here | What it covers | |---|---|---| | | [Quick Start](https://estellaengine.com/docs/getting-started/quick-start/) | install the editor, make a project, press play | | | [ECS](https://estellaengine.com/docs/core-concepts/ecs/) | components, systems and queries — how game logic is written | | | [AI Agents](https://estellaengine.com/docs/agents/mcp/) | connect Claude Code, Cursor or Codex to the editor | | | [Time of Day](https://estellaengine.com/docs/graphics/time-of-day/) | a sun and sky that follow the clock | | | [Weather](https://estellaengine.com/docs/graphics/weather/) | mist, rain and snow | | | [Exporting](https://estellaengine.com/docs/publishing/overview/) | web, desktop, playable ads and the rest, from one project | | | [Mini-game platforms](https://estellaengine.com/docs/publishing/minigame-platforms/) | WeChat, Douyin, Kuaishou, Bilibili, Alipay, Huawei | | | [Android & iOS](https://estellaengine.com/docs/publishing/android-ios/) | native arm64 apps | ## Feedback Estella does not accept pull requests. Bug reports and feature requests are welcome as [issues](https://github.com/esengine/estella/issues) — see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for what to include, and for building the engine from source. Maintainers: see the [release procedure](RELEASING.md) for candidate builds, acceptance evidence and publishing. ## License The engine runtime, SDK, asset pipeline, CLI, project templates and editor plugin API in this repository are licensed under the [Apache License, Version 2.0](LICENSE) — free for any purpose, commercial use included. We follow [Semantic Versioning](VERSIONING.md) and keep a [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md). - **The visual editor** is a separate, free product built on this engine; its source is not public. Everything needed to build, run and ship a game is here — see [BUSINESS_MODEL.md](BUSINESS_MODEL.md). - **Trademarks.** The license covers the code, not the "Estella" / "ESEngine" names or logos: say your project uses Estella, but don't ship a fork under that name. - **Spine.** The bundled [Spine Runtimes](third_party) are not open source; a game that uses Estella's Spine integration needs its own Spine license. See [NOTICE](NOTICE).
